utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, we are -- we are in Court. Please take ... Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sit down. Mr. Lukic, may you please make sure that you control your client. Madam Registrar, would you please -- Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. I'm sorry about all the confusion at the beginning. And thank you, Madam Registrar, for calling the case. I am made to understand that there is a new member of staff on the side of the Defence, and for that reason I'm going to ask just for the parties to state their appearances for the day, starting with you, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, I am Dermot Groome. I am with Edward Jeremy and we're being assisted today by Ms. Janet Stewart and Ms. Bojana Vuleta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And on the Defence side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic, Miodrag Stojanovic, Milos Saljic, Sasa Lukic, and Dan Ivetic will be -- is with us, sorry, but on the wrong place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Before we call the witness, I believe that the parties have -- well, the Prosecution has an issue to raise, so does the Chamber, but let's hear you first, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, yesterday evening we received notice of the documents the Defence intends to put to Mr. van Lynden. Many of these documents are original B/C/S documents for which there is no English translation in e-court nor has one been provided by other means by the Defence. Out of the approximately 40 documents, over 30 we are unable to find English translations for. So prior to the continuation of the cross-examination, the Prosecution request that Mr. Lukic state how he intends to use these documents with the witness, particularly in light of the evidence provided by the witness yesterday that he does not speak Serbo-Croatian. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To be honest with you, Your Honours, I didn't know that we have that many untranslated documents, especially since all of them were acquired through Tribunal's electronic systems and were actually found either on EDS or among our documents. So I'm really not aware. We'll see if I'm going to use any of untranslated documents, because we enumerated much more documents that we are going really to use with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's -- that may very well be so, Mr. Lukic, but, you know, it is your responsibility as a cross-examining counsel to make sure that whatever documents you are going to use are available in the official languages of the Tribunal, particularly because you do know that you opposite number and the witness do not speak Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will do my best to avoid using documents that are not translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. The Chamber appreciates that, Mr. Lukic. May the Chamber may then move into discussing what it has as its own issues. Yesterday in court, the Chamber put on the record its instruction of 30th May 2012 for the Prosecution to review its 92 bis motion for Witness RM057 in light of a number of adjudicated facts. The Chamber also sought an update from the Prosecution on that matter. The Prosecution indicated informally that it may be able to provide this update today. Mr. Groome, is the Prosecution in a position to do so?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]... hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yesterday evening, Your Honour, I reviewed this issue with respect to RM057. The bulk of the evidence this witness would be able to provide this Chamber, should his evidence be adduced, is in fact covered by the Trial Chamber having taken judicial notice of previously adjudicated facts. The Prosecution is still in the process of assessing whether this witness's evidence related to the identification of victims is necessary to meet our burden with respect to establishing the death of specific witnesses. This assessment can only be completed once an expert we have retained completes her work. In light of this, the Prosecution will be filing this week an application to withdraw the applications now pending before the Chamber with respect to RM057 and will, at the appropriate time in the future, file a notice that we will either not adduce this evidence or the evidence of this witness in reliance on adjudicated facts or should it be necessary an application to adduce that portion of the witness's evidence that is necessary or remains necessary to establish proof of death under Rule 92 bis. And that will be filed before the end of the week, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Groome. Next, again, yesterday, the Chamber asked for an update in relation to MFIs D27 to D37 tendered through Witness Schmitz for which a B/C/S translation is missing. The Defence submitted it could not approach CLSS for a B/C/S translation. The Prosecution submitted it may have B/C/S translations of some of these exhibits and that it would further discuss this matter with the Defence. Mr. Groome, are you able to update us on whether you have had any discussions with the Defence and, if so, what the outcome of them are.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, on behalf of the Prosecution, Ms. Stewart, I believe, met with Mr. Lukic prior to the Court or the Chamber entering today, and I will defer to my colleague to maybe update the Chamber on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What I can say, Your Honours, is that Ms. Stewart was surprised, the same way as we are, that we cannot ask translation into B/C/S from CLSS since their explanation is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber is equally surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since the official languages of this Tribunal are English and French and they don't want to translate into B/C/S. Unless they changed their policy in last two, three weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Lukic, I'm going to ask you to please advise Mr. Mladic we are in court and that if he does have anything to talk to you about or to anyone of your team, he must do so as softly and quietly as possible and in an unintrusive manner. Please keep him under control. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I saw you standing up. I don't know whether you had any contribution to make on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, simply to observe in the ten years I've been practicing before this Tribunal this is the first I have ever become aware that CLSS would not translate a document. Perhaps it might be worth the Chamber making inquiry with CLSS to see has there been some misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. That's what Judge Fluegge and I were just talking about right now as you stood up, because we are equally surprised by this kind of conduct. Be that as it may, are there any strong objections from the Prosecution for admission of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I believe you're tending them for admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think so. We did tender them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They are so admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. We now may call the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. van Lynden.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hope you had a restful night yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I turn you over to Mr. Lukic may the record once again, Madam Registrar, please show that the Chamber continues to sit pursuant to Rule 15 bis for the same reasons as were mentioned yesterday. And secondly to you, Mr. van Lynden, to remind you - I know that you do not need any reminding but I do so. I'm obliged to do so - that you're still bound by the declaration made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the witness is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, good morning, Mr. van Lynden.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have your statement before you?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We left off at paragraph 26 yesterday. You say you had never seen with your own eyes anybody killed by a sniper but you saw civilians die soon after they were shot by a sniper, and you describe a case involving two men and one woman, all dressed in civilian clothing. Could we agree that in the time described here there were a lot of armed people wearing civilian clothes in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were armed people wearing civilian clothes in Sarajevo in July 1992, but there were also uniformed. And at that particular scene, what I remember were actually people in police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we also agree that you do not know the ethnicity of the wounded people or the identity of those who shot them?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ethnicity, you actually mean the religion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because ethnicity, everybody in Bosnia, as far as I am aware, was a Slav. No, I don't. When we -- we -- we followed them to the -- they were taken -- two men as I recall, were taken to the morgue of the Kosevo hospital, the academic hospital of Sarajevo, and I do not recall that they had papers on them identifying who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll now move to paragraph 29 of your statement. You said during the periods I stayed in Pale there was electricity cuts. There were electricity cuts at time but there was always running water. Pale is a small place so I'd like you to compare the situation in the parts of Sarajevo held by the Serbs regarding electricity, for instance?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't stay in the areas of Sarajevo held by the Serbs. I was brought there only during the day, but I stayed at night in Pale. These were day visits. And whether they had electricity or not, I -- I cannot now recall. I didn't stay there in a house. And we were taken to military positions there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you don't know what the situation was like with water either in those parts of town.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my visits there, I do not recall that those who accompanied me from the Bosnian Serb government, because we were always accompanied, made any references to the lack of water or electricity in those parts of Sarajevo held by the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That doesn't mean there was electricity or running water; correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now paragraph 30. You talk about nutrition in war and how it affects the population. You talk about food supplies. You personally were not able to make any inquiries; correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We made inquiries with the UNHCR and with the Bosnian government as to food supplies. This was in Sarajevo, the parts of Sarajevo held by the Bosnian government, and we spoke to experts at the academic hospital, also at the former military hospital, people who were experts in -- in nutrition. I think I mention in my statement also the head of the maternity part of the Kosevo hospital who gave us figures on, for instance, still-born babies and that the babies that were born were of less weight than was normally, and therefore they thought those were the consequences, the direct consequences of the civilian population not having the same nutrition as they had done in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the situation in the Serbian parts of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, we were not in a position to do the same research there. We spent -- specifically the research that I mention here in this paragraph, Your Honours, was done in November, December, 1992. In September 1992 when I worked from Pale, we did ask and we actually saw the distribution of, for instance, money to pensioners, and we filmed this, and also that there were certain shops open for the civilian population. I would immediately say that the amount of pension that pensioners could get was very small, that their situation was very difficult but we saw, for instance, in one particular shop in Grbavica that there were oranges on sale, and this was absolutely not the case in the other side of the front lines in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I do not want to interfere with your cross-examination, but just for the Chamber's understanding of your cross-examination, is it your case that there's a distinction to be made between Serb civilians and non-Serb civilians, or is it your case that civilians were in want, on the one hand, and at the expense of or because of the conduct of the armies, either army, whatever the army may be? My question really is: Does it matter whether they are Serbs, or does it -- or what --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Exactly Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What matters is it not that they are civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Our position is that division shouldn't have been done or both parts should be examined and compared. But obviously it wasn't done at that time. That's -- that's what we want to point out to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the same paragraph as you mentioned, you say you visited the head of the maternity word in the Kosevo hospital. I'd like to ask you: Did you seek the same information on the Serbian side? Were you interested at all in the position of the civilian population in the parts of town held by the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did. We asked in Pale. The -- we were taken to one hospital, not within Sarajevo, but -- I have to try to recall the name. I think it was called Sokolac. This was a -- had been a mental institution but there was a new wing built that was turned into a hospital and we were taken there and we spoke to the doctors there. But from what we gathered there, and what we saw, the wounded that were being treated there were all Bosnian Serb military.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Precisely. What about the civilians in Sarajevo? You did not do any research into their situation, did you, in the parts of town held by the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have just said that we had requested but that this request was not fulfilled by the authorities in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know it's been a long time, but do you know from whom you made this request? Was it in writing? Could we locate that letter in your correspondence? Or did you make a verbal request?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't make any requests in writing. The requests were made in conversations that my field producer and I had with Mr. Karadzic at -- at his headquarters in Pale. We had various meetings -- they were not official interviews, they were just meetings, and there we put our requests as to what we wanted to see and who we wanted to meet and what was possible. And some of those requests were met, including the interview that we had with Mr. Mladic, and certain requests were not met. And although we were taken into Grbavica, we had asked specifically to look into also the plight of the civilian population, and that was not a request that was met.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now paragraph 31 of your statement, please. You say in May 1992: "On my second or third day in Sarajevo, I went with my cameraman to what had been the former JNA hospital ..." Was there any damage to the facade of the hospital when you just arrived?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say in my statement, it was very badly shot up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear it was shot at while it was occupied by members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The hospital where you stayed, the former military or State Hospital which is its alternative name, was in the vicinity of the Marsal Tito barracks in Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And it was close to the front line near Grbavica; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would judge the front lines to have been about 500 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now paragraph 33 of your statement: "While I was at the State Hospital, I never saw any evidence that Bosnian snipers fired from there." You do not know whether snipers fired from there when you were not at the hospital, to begin with; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, clearly, I don't know for concern, no. We did ask repeatedly. As I mentioned to the Court yesterday, I was responsible also for the welfare of the television crew I brought with me, and bringing them to a location that was also used by the military would obviously put their lives under a greater threat than they already were than being in a war zone, and I, at no time, was told that those buildings were used by snipers of the Bosnian army. And we also checked for any kind of evidence in the form of spent cartridges to see, and we never found any evidence of any sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it your evidence today that you inspected the entire hospital to make sure? And how often did you do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where does that come from, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, what? Where does it come from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Inspection. The witness has never spoken about inspection. He says he just checked for casings of cartridges.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking him how often and where. Where he checked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can ask that question. But to say, Is it your evidence today that you made inspections, you're suggesting that that is the evidence he has made, he has given. Line 24 of page 12. "Is it your evidence today that you inspected the entire hospital to make sure?"

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is not the evidence that he has given.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Tell us, then, how you checked that hospital building and how often. Which floors did you inspect; which wards; who did the inspection?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the periods that I was in Sarajevo, specifically in 1992, we were in the hospital practically every single -- from late afternoon onwards and then throughout the night. We made our base, as I have testified yesterday, right on the top floor of the building where there was no one else. There were -- the wards were empty. Indeed, the wards on all the top floors of the hospital were empty. They were no longer being used. Only the lower floors were in use. On the top floor, of course, we looked around, because we -- we were working on both sides of the building. We, of course, also entered at casualty every day and saw the situation there. I didn't go on an inspection. This is a war zone, and I was working, but we did check the building. I did check the building on several occasions. Also, the parts of the building that are not the main building that we were in but other parts sometimes because we wanted to film damage that had been done by shelling. Sometimes because we were meeting certain doctors as, for instance, the nutritional specialists that we talked about earlier, they were in another part of the building with laboratories there, and we talked to them. And I always made a point of asking everyone I met and who worked in the building. And throughout the war, there were Muslims, Catholics and Orthodox working within the former military hospital, whether it had been used for military purposes. I had to, also, because I was responsible for my crew and had to keep them as safe as possible in that war zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there any sniper fire, fire from tanks or mortars from the Marsal Tito barracks, which was very close to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never witnessed any fire from tanks or mortars. From the Marsal Tito barracks?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw tank fire or mortar fire from the Marsal Tito barracks. You're referring to the period after they had been evacuated by the Bosnian army -- Bosnian Serb army. I did on one occasion see not sniper fire but machine-gun fire emanating from one window of the Marsal Tito barracks. This is in -- in reference to the incident that we have actually already talked about in paragraph 26. And I actually say there, I then heard shots coming from the Marsal Tito barracks and I could see gun smoke from a weapon being fired from that. It was not a sniper. It was a machine-gun. And on that occasion, I think it was giving covering fire for those trying to recover the bodies in the street. But back to your original question, no, I did not see tank or mortar fire from the Marsal Tito barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you see a tank firing from behind Marsal Tito barracks, between the barracks and the railway station?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And if we had, we would have filmed it. So that my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is military documentation about that, but I'm not going to show it because you've never seen these documents. At any rate, we can agree that nobody ever made any reports to you about the points in the city of Sarajevo where the soldiers of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina fired from.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's -- we can't agree on that because I was actually taken to certain front lines by the Bosnian army at certain parts of -- of Sarajevo. Obviously not everywhere, but I was taken, on certain occasions, to certain front lines where we did film. For instance --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I beg your pardon. Just a moment, please. Perhaps I wasn't clear enough in putting my question. Perhaps I did not put it properly. You did not receive information, daily information, that would make it possible for you to know where the members of the army in Bosnia-Herzegovina were shooting from. Do you know all the positions in town from which the members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina were firing?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But you would never know that in any war on either side. I wouldn't know that from the Bosnian Serb side either. I wouldn't have known that in Beirut on either side of the green line. One doesn't get that kind of information from any army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Precisely. Thank you. Multiple rocket-launchers are quite easily noticeable. Did you see any in Sarajevo; and did you see any, say, in Grancevica? One was there. Did you see any firing at Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my time in Sarajevo, I never saw a multiple rocket-launcher. Again, if we had done, we would have filmed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While you were in hospital, you say that that is where your crew was, and you say that you were responsible for them. You consider that hospital to be safe, right, that's the explanation you gave us, especially the upper floors?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's a building in a war zone, so nowhere is safe. My principal interest in being there is that we could work as effectively as possible from that building because it afforded as a view, as I described yesterday in court. The other reason why it was for us a relatively comfortable place to work is because it was a hospital. There was water and electricity there. I personally believe that working on the top floor, as I think I also explained to the Court yesterday, was, I believe, relatively safe because if that building was going to be targeted, people would aim at the middle rather than at the top floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And were any of your crew members ever wounded? Were you personally wounded in that hospital?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of my crew members nor I were ever wounded in the hospital, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank God. Also, in paragraph 35. 35. You said that from the area around Sarajevo multiple rocket-launcher fire came from the top of the mountains around Sarajevo and falling very close to the hospital --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, we did not hear the end of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the interpreters did not hear the end of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the end of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was: The hospital was never hit from these artillery pieces; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whilst I was in the building, I am not aware of the hospital ever being hit by multiple rocket fire. No. The only thing - and I do mention this - that there was in November 1992 a large explosion and one of the lift shafts was hit. I can't verify what it was hit by, but others told us that they thought that this was a tank shell. But I didn't personally see that. I was in the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From these upper floors of the hospital, did you see that the launchers of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were positioned behind the Marsal Tito barracks and were firing from there for quite a while?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you would have to be more precise as to the dates that this occurred. And, no, again, I think I have already answered this question. No, they didn't. And if they had while we were there, we would have been able to film it, and we were never able to film something like that. So it didn't occur at least in the periods in Sarajevo when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said: "In my opinion, it was probably a tank shell because the local people who saw it fall on the hospital said that it fell directly which is characteristic for -- for tank shells." First of all, if there was a trajectory, you did not see it yourself. You heard about it from others; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already stated that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can also agree that you are not a military expert, although you did your military service for all of two years. You were never a member of a tank crew. So these are two questions: You are not a military expert; right? And you were never a member of a tank crew; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depends how you define military expert. I spent 23 years going to war zones watching militias, guerillas, and armies fighting wars. I have never been a member of a tank crew. But I have been with tanks when they fired, during the Iran-Iraq war and again during the first Gulf War, all of which preceded the war in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go back to this now. Do you consider yourself to be a military expert, qualified enough to testify in an expert manner about military matters?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would call myself a war correspondent with a lot of experience in war, but to say that I was a military expert with expertise on every single kind of weaponry, no, I wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, have you been called here as an expert witness, as a military expert?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No -- not to my knowledge, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 36 now, please. You say that you crossed the front line. That was allowed by both sides, wasn't it, by the Army of Republika Srpska and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could civilians move about that way?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: By that stage of the war, not as far as I'm aware, and I did not witness that, apart from on one occasion, which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You heard about that. Thank you. Could the Serbs leave Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those Serbs living in Grbavica and the territory held by the Bosnian Serbs, yes. Those within the part of Sarajevo held by the Bosnians, not immediately, although I am aware of certain exchanges being made, and we, in fact, even filmed one of a Muslim woman crossing over from Grbavica into Sarajevo proper. And I am aware of others, including certain members of -- who became senior members of Mr. Karadzic's staff who had initially been in Sarajevo and in the June, July, August were able to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. Lukic, may I interrupt here. Mr. van Lynden, at page 19, line 25, you're giving an answer to a question which said, the question was: "Could civilians move about that way?" And you give an answer by saying: "By that stage of the war, not as far as I am aware, and I did not witness that, apart from on one occasion which is --" And then you were interrupted by Mr. Lukic who said: "You heard about that. Thank you. " And I don't see anything that suggests that you heard anything from your answer. So I think, for that reason, I would like to make sure that you complete your answer. Can you answer that question, please, fully.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. What I was going to say was that when in September 1992 we were taken to Grbavica, we actually witnessed and were able to film a Bosnian Muslim woman. We were told -- didn't actually personally meet her, but she was crossing from Grbavica on a small bridge to the other side, over -- across the river Miljacka into the other side of Sarajevo. That is one occasion. We were told by the Bosnian Serb soldiers that we were with that this had been arranged. I imagine that more of such instances did occur but that we were obviously not always there to film them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What had been arranged, the crossing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That this one women, a quite elderly women as I recall, would be allowed to leave the Bosnian Serb-held territory and cross over into the territory held by the Bosnian government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That completes your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That completes my answer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You may proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question, once again, probably had not been put well enough, because this is what I wanted to ask you. I wanted to ask you whether thousands of Serbs who were in the territory that was held by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were able to leave that part of the Sarajevo and go to the territory that was held by the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know the precise numbers that were able to leave. I am aware, as I already said, that certain people, including people who became senior staff members of Mr. Karadzic were able to leave Sarajevo. The precise manner of their leaving, I am not aware of. Whether they had do this by night or whether there was agreement between the two sides that certain people could leave and other people could enter. I don't know how many people left. I am aware that later on in the war quite a lot of the civilians living in Sarajevo tried to get out by crossing the airport, which was then under UN control and getting out of Sarajevo in that manner. But, again, I don't have figures as to how many people tried or managed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were in Sarajevo for a long time. Did you hear who it was that was preventing civilians from leaving Sarajevo, regardless of whether these were Serbs or Croats or Muslims? Were they prevented from doing so by Croats, Serbs, or the Muslim authorities? Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a war zone. It's a front line of a besieged city. You can't just cross that on foot. As I also testified yesterday, just crossing initially in a car, later on, we had armoured Land Rovers because every time we crossed front lines we were shot at as well. It's a basic rule in any war: You don't cross front lines. And for civilians caught up in the situation, it was obviously very, very difficult. And no, I'm not -- if -- if there were certain deals done I am aware of that but the precise nature of the deals were not revealed to me by either sides in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you've testified yourself there were periods when there were cease-fires. Actually, I'm going to be specific on this. Do you know that the Muslim authorities in Sarajevo did not allow civilians to leave the city of Sarajevo, irrespective of their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that because -- I know of civilians who were allowed to leave Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are speaking of a few civilians, but I'm talking about tens of thousands of civilians who wanted to leave Sarajevo and were not allowed to do so. If you know about it, please tell us about it; if you do not, we're just going to move on.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that case, I would suggest that you move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you. [Interpretation] You were in Srebrenica, too. Did you hear about that from civilians there, that the authorities from Sarajevo would not allow civilians from Srebrenica to leave Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was in Srebrenica one day, if I'm right in November 1992, with the first UN aid convoy. We were allowed to enter. We were there for a number of hours. We did speak to some of the civilians there. These were all people who had fled to Srebrenica because they had been hounded out of the other towns and villages of Eastern Bosnia. They had sought refuge there. I didn't meet anyone in Srebrenica who said that the Bosnian authorities wouldn't let them leave. They were surrounded by what they considered to be their enemies. And, therefore, I'm sure that if they could have got out of their situation living in a besieged enclave with too little food and very, very little medical supplies at all - there was no hospital in Srebrenica just a clinic - they would have wanted to leave. But I have never heard, at that stage, from any of them that this was the Bosnian authorities that were stopping them from doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In Bosnia, you hadn't heard of overcrowded UNPROFOR buses and trucks that civilians from Srebrenica were trying to get onto in order to leave Srebrenica. Also, you did not hear that such convoys, were, afterwards, banned by the Sarajevo authorities. Also, did you not hear that they had no problem whatsoever with the Serb army and Serb authorities, that that they would allow them to leave Srebrenica. You never heard of any of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: A number of questions in that, Mr. Lukic. I'm not quite sure which one you want the witness to answer. Could you take them one by one, please. Start with the overcrowded UNPROFOR buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of civilians from Srebrenica being taken out of Srebrenica by UNPROFOR on trucks and they were so overcrowded that some persons even died in the process?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, is it possible to get a time-frame about when we are speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. [Interpretation] During 1993, the spring of 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My first comment would be is you asked me if I had been to Srebrenica and I answered that I had went in with the very first UN convoy that was allowed after being held up repeatedly by the Bosnian Serb army into Srebrenica. There was no case on that occasion of any civilian getting on any truck. Absolutely not. The convoy came in. They unloaded. They only had flour with them, as I recall, and then they drove back to -- back to Zvornik, if I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What year was that, Mr. van Lynden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Late 1992, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not 1993 that the question is about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first question I was asked by Mr. Lukic was that I had been, myself, to Srebrenica. In relation to the events of 1993 [Realtime transcript read in error "1992"], I was not in Srebrenica in 1993 [Realtime transcript read in error "1992"]. I did manage to go to Gorazde. I was not in a position because we were ourselves in the field reporting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. van Lynden. I'm going to -- the transcription on the record says: In relation to 1992. I was not in Srebrenica in 1992." I thought I heard something different.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in 1992, I did enter Srebrenica. In 1993 I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This sentence in relation to 1990 [sic] we were talking about 1993, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right. That's what I'm trying to correct because the record is 1992 when you're talking 1993. So you are saying in relation to 1993, you were not in Srebrenica in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you as a war correspondent whether you heard about that and whether you reported on it, if you had heard about it.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did hear about it. But I heard about it after the fact because I was elsewhere reporting on other matters. As far as I am aware, a television crew and I think a British television crew was in Srebrenica at the time and those pictures were shown. But, as I said, I was not in a position to watch them because I was in another part of the country where there was no electricity and no television to watch. So we were aware of it but later, at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since you heard that they were leaving, did you also hear that civilians were forbidden from leaving Srebrenica and that it was the Muslim authorities in Sarajevo that had forbidden them to do that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I am aware - but, again, I didn't cover this personally - civilians were allowed to leave at a certain stage and whether they were later forbidden to and whom they were forbidden by, I am not aware. But I would add here that I was in another enclave, Gorazde, at just about the same period that you are referring to in 1993, and there I personally witnessed every single night civilians from within the Gorazde enclave walking through the Serbs' lines, besieging them to their own lines, and they were allowed to do that. Most of those civilians did that to get food and then returned the following night. But many, specifically the older and the young, were then taken by the Bosnian army to refugee camps in Central Bosnia. As far as I am aware that was never stopped. I never saw anyone from the Bosnian authorities stopping them doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that the time for the first break is upon us. Before the Chamber does rise, I would ask -- the next witness is on stand by. It would be appreciated if the Prosecution could have some indication of how long the examination of this witness is likely to be and when the Chamber would like to have the next witness in the waiting-room ready to take the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, are you able to help us?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. When I was calculating how much time I needed for this witness, my rough calculation was 14 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] 14 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. So I used two and a half hours by now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which is what the Chamber has sort of guesstimated as cross-examining period for a witness that was taken for 90 minutes by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't have actually strict guidance, as you know, at least yet. So before -- half an hour we were supposed to have two and a half hours of cross-examination. This gentleman has a lot of videos, and we really cannot cover all this pretty long statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. But if -- for 30 minutes, you have two and a half hours, you wouldn't have 14 hours for 90 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would have seven and a half hours, but ... I ask for your leave to cross this witness longer than it was supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you ask Mr. Mladic to understand that we are in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm trying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You know, if he doesn't understand, the Chamber, at some stage is going to get him out of the court. May he please understand that, because we are in court. We demand order in court, okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please try to tell him that during the break. We're going to take a break, and we will come to decide on this issue when we come back. We'll come back at 20 past. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, before the witness comes in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we can go to a private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Madam Registrar. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the end of the previous session, Your Honours, you asked me why do we need more time for cross of this witness. And, first of all, this witness was scheduled for hour and a half in direct, apart from his statement, and, actually, he spend two hours in that direct. And two and a half hours were envisaged if five documents were introduced through the witness, and if the Prosecution spends half an hour leading that witness. We have, with this witness, I -- because we had several lists, but I think that we have around 20 or more exhibits, mostly videos with this witness, introduced through him, and the Prosecution spent two hours leading him. So we are not even with only our calculations, we are not on seven and a half but at ten hours, since it's four times more than the original ones. Plus extra evidence introduced through the witness. So I would kindly ask Your Honours to have this in mind when deciding how much time you will allocate to our team to cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: First of all, let me say to you I'm not quite sure how you come to ten hours. If we use the mathematical calculation that you used --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Two hours and four times more than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Two hours, times four; I understand that. But you also understand that this is not a hard and fast rule. This is a case by case situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you have to look at how the cross-examination is going. You spent quite a bit of time yesterday cross-examining this witness about the war in Afghanistan, the relevance of which the Chamber did ask you about, and you indicated that you wanted to show the relationship between the witness and the Mujahedin, which we never saw, okay? Today, you're asking him questions about whether he is a military expert. Again, he is not called as a military expert, and I don't know where you're going with those kind of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just wanted him to say: No I'm not. Then he elaborated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You know he is not called as a military expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But he acts as one. He wants to explain us many military issues, so I just wanted to establish that he is not, and tomorrow when we address his testimony we have clearly that even he knows he is [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you can tell him. If you cross-examine in a focussed manner, you tell him: You are not an expert -- a military expert, are you not? And that disposes of the question. You don't waste time on that, okay? I'm not quite sure whether it is your intention, Mr. Lukic, to go paragraph by paragraph through this lengthy statement, and are you saying that you are disputing every little paragraph or are you saying there are issues that you dispute and that you are going to go into and look at. You've just gone by paragraph by paragraph with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because he is addressing many issues, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that he may be addressing many issues. But are they all issues that you take issue -- on a paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not all of them, of course. Not all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're going through the paragraphs seriatim.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know how else should I go through them, unless that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought you would go through the points that you differ with or those points that you would like to elucidate or those points that you dispute. Anyway, the Chamber will give you the next two sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Cross of this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's not possible, Your Honour. Trust me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You go ahead, and let's see how you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please be called in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you carry on, Mr. Lukic, something has just been brought to the attention of the Chamber, which I would like to make you aware of. It's a -- it's -- it's a note written to the Registrar here. It says: "As I'm sure you are already aware, the accused has again made comments about the witness and even though the witness is coping well with this, he informed me that he feels it quite inappropriate that a witness is subjected to comments and accusations by the accused in the courtroom and he wishes the Chamber to be aware of his feelings on this matter." Now, both of Judge Fluegge and I do not understand Serbo-Croatian. This is a remark that comes from now -- I think this is from Victims and Witness Section. This is a -- I'm asking you to attend to this, as you understand the language better than we do, and, again, warn your client that he must desist from making comments about the witness, particularly in the courtroom while the case is going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at document 1D137 in e-court, please. And before we get the document, you told us that in early June 1992, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was not an army in the proper sense of that word. Can we have an English version of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: English version of document is not available in e-court, Your Honours. It looks like it's not released.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can find it in ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That means that it is not released. You can open it, but we cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe that's why we cannot see translations, and maybe that's why the Prosecution objected. I don't know. We loaded English translations as well. But I can read from English version, so we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think you just should release the document so that it is available for the Prosecution and the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We cannot release. There are two parts of releasing the documents. First, our Case Manager releases it; and then ITSS, the electronics, the Tribunal electronics system has to release it, then [indiscernible] as well, so only after those two steps we can see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You indicated earlier, Mr. Lukic, earlier before the break that you are going to try to keep away from documents that are not translated. You're going to keep documents that have an English translation. How do we deal with this? We can't -- we don't know what is written here. We've got to have --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We had a lot of problems last week. On Friday, they promised they will solve the problem. Obviously they haven't. It is absolutely not our fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. But I'm talking about what you told us this morning, that you were not going to use documents that have no translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This one does. And we have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Give us the translation. Give us the translation. If it is it there, give it to us. If we can't see it here, then we don't have it. To say it's there, it doesn't help us because we can't access it. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask that until the technical problem is resolved that Mr. Lukic ask one of his staff to print hard copies of it so that we can follow along in that manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At least that can be done. I mean that's an obvious step -- solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will send a message to our staff to do photocopy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't you have hard copies of the document here?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have it for me. Your Honour, I did not know that it is not released. I don't deal with the technical side of this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, once again, to upload the document is the first step and the second is to release it to the other party, to the opposing party, and to the Chamber. And it's the responsibility of the party to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. But when we release it, then the electronic system of the Tribunal run by the Tribunal employees have to release it also, further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. But have you released it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes we have. We can see it on our screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's on your screens?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But you must take care of this process. It is your responsibility to make available the translation to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours [overlapping speakers] the Tribunal are not my responsibility. My responsibility are people from my team, not people from the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So they haven't done their job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You are in contact with those who are in charge of these matters, not the Chamber, not the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Exactly. They promised us that everything would be solved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The problem here is, Mr. Lukic, that you may very well not be responsible for Tribunal staff but you are responsible for seeing that the evidence you want to present to the Court is available to the Court when you want it to be presented to the Court. And if you realise that the staff of the Tribunal has not done so, you make sure that they follow up and do so before you call your witness or before you call the document. So the responsibility is still yours to make sure that when you come into court, you are able to communicate with the Chamber in a language that the Chamber understands, and the official language of the Chamber is either English or French.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can move on and return to these documents, if I have a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify something. Yesterday you were saying how General Mladic took, grabbed you in the face. Can you tell us if there is any kind of video record or any photograph of that, please.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I also mentioned to the Court yesterday, this occurred while both the cameraman of Sky News and the cameraman of the BBC were in the room where the upper military council, or whatever the name may have been of the Bosnian Serbs, was meeting. All the other members of that group were already in the room. That's where the two cameramen and the two producers were. The person who was with me, the other outsider, if you like, was John Simpson of the BBC. I am aware that John has actually reported about this incident a year ago, at the time that Mr. Mladic was brought to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The name of this John, please?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: John Simpson. He's the senior foreign correspondent of the BBC.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you say the producers were there as well. Was one of your producers also present? Which one, if so?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said was that the producers were with the cameramen in a separate room. The producer who was working with me at the time was Jaksic Cekic, who was our Belgrade bureau chief at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm trying to cut things short now. Paragraph 53, you say: "In another story, also broadcast in earlier June, I said that I believed that Sarajevo was being deliberately obliterated because of what we were seeing." Has Sarajevo been obliterated? Can we agree that it was not?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sarajevo was very severely shelled. Obliterated in the sense that it was completely wiped off the map, no, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So it was more of a journalistic literally -- literary expression; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the expression that came to mind at that time, after I had witnessed those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And, again, in the same paragraph, you say: "No particular spot was being targeted; these projectiles were hitting right across the city. I felt that the whole city was being targeted." And about this, I want to ask you: Again, you didn't know the disposition of the forces of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina within Sarajevo from where they opened fire at Serb positions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I had been taken to a number of front line positions but I was not aware of all the positions of the Bosnian army within Sarajevo, no; indeed, at no point throughout the war. And that is situation, really, with any armed forces in any conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After the JNA left the Marsal Tito barracks, who moved in? And did anyone move in?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I imagine that, although we didn't actually film them moving in, that members of the Bosnian army moved in. We were told that military equipment had been left there, and in one of the stories that was shown to the Court yesterday, we filmed and showed in that story people running out of the Marsal Tito barracks after its evacuation. So those were some of those people who went in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know if any other barracks in Sarajevo and its environs were transferred or got into the hands of the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never taken to another barracks within Sarajevo by the Bosnian army. I am aware that there were other barracks and that those must have been taken over by the Bosnian army. The manner in which they used them, I don't know, because I did not actually personally witness that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were in the hospital, which is very close to the barracks. Do you know what happened to the soldiers who were guarding that hospital? Do you know that they were killed, all the members of the JNA who were guarding the army when the hospital was taken over by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware that the hospital was ever taken over by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Whilst I was there, it was run by the same people who had been running it before then, and that included Bosnian Serbs and Bosnian Croats, senior surgeons. The director of the hospital when I arrived was Bakir Nakas. And I had been told that he was the director previously. And when I arrived in Sarajevo, there were no guards guarding the hospital and I was not made aware of what -- what you suggest. The only thing I am aware of is when I arrived in May 1992, there was at least one soldier of the JNA who had been wounded who was being taken care of in that hospital. One soldier wounded in the Marsal Tito barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you're saying that the same people worked in the hospital as they did before the war. Is that this case everywhere in Bosnia and Herzegovina because no side wanted to give up their doctors? The doctors are needed more in war time. So did you go to other hospitals and did you see that the same cadre remained before the war, that people were simply not leaving?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was a difference between the former military hospital and, for instance, the Kosevo hospital which is actually the main academic hospital of Sarajevo, that their people did leave, doctors. I didn't personally see them leave. But we were informed that some of the staff that had been there previously had left that hospital. I'm aware that in other parts of Bosnia that I visited, for instance, Gorazde, doctors were sent in from Sarajevo to man that hospital, including at least two doctors from the former military hospital because I had met them there before, and then encountered them again when I went into Gorazde. The doctors that I met at the one hospital that was run by the Bosnian Serbs that I mentioned earlier this morning, if I remember correctly at Sokolac, they had come from various places, including Sarajevo, and they had clearly made a conscious choice to leave Sarajevo and then work there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 55 of your statement, please. I'd like to ask you: Were you in Sarajevo when the JNA left the Marsal Tito barracks? What date was it? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there. And we actually filmed the first buses, as I remember, with soldiers at the end of the afternoon - there was a long day of negotiation - leaving the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that the end of May or the beginning of June?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it -- the beginning of June. We had a night with the a lot of artillery -- a lot of shelling. And the next day was strange for us because it was suddenly completely silent, and we were actually able to walk along streets where we would not have dared walk the previous day, and the negotiations actually took place by the front gate, and we were able to film that prior to the departure of the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 58. You told us you were not an artillery man. You had the training in handling the mortar, and during the Desert Storm you spent a lot of time with American artillery units. Could we agree that the American artillery and the Serbian artillery at the time did not act in the same way. First of all, the Serbs don't have satellites to guide their rockets or missiles or shells, and they don't have the machinery and the precision of fire that the Americans had; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to whether this is within the scope of the witness's ability to answer the question. I'm not sure there's been any basis established for what American military hardware consisted of or Serbian military hardware consists of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then we cannot use paragraph 58 or any of his estimates and comparisons. If the Prosecution is willing to strike the paragraphs that deal with these matters in this statement. We are happy to continue without them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is nothing in that paragraph about satellite capability and satellite guided missiles. It is very concrete observations of what the witness saw in his time in Iraq and his time in Bosnia and I submit that he is confident to talk about his own personal observations in the context of his own personal training but he is certainly not within -- that I'm aware of, his scope of knowledge, these broader questions about sophisticated equipment that the Americans may or may not have.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll formulate my question according to the statement the Prosecutor just gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. van Lynden, you are not qualified enough, as the Prosecutor suggests, to know how the American army operates; correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Why -- you -- you read paragraph 58 of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Why don't you stick to that information and ask the witness about the content of his statement? Now is a very broad question again, if he knows the American army -- how the American army operates. What is that, how the American army operates? Can you please focus on what he is giving in his statement and put a precise question to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. In his statement the witness says: "The senior officers commanding these units explained to me then exactly how such an artillery battery operates and what its purpose is." If the witness knows precisely what kind of artillery battery is operating, then he should be able to answer exactly how it operates, whether satellites are used, whether laser guidance is used because he knows exactly how the unit operates. I'm asking him if he knows. And my question was only about the usage of satellites, lasers, and such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I don't agree with you. The quotation you have put on the records shows "the senior officers commanding these units explained to me." This is absolutely different from his personal knowledge. He is testifying about what others told him. You should be very precise in putting questions to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What did US commanders explain to you? How does it work? What kind of technology were they using?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It -- it wasn't about the technology. It was about the use of where the shells landed in a military context. They didn't explain the precise technology involved - and I wouldn't really expect military officers to do that - but what its function was in any operation, either defensive or offensive. And that's what I'm referring to in -- in this paragraph. And there they explained about -- which I knew because with mortars it's the same thing about shells landing too long or too short when you are trying to find a target until a target is found and then there is sustained fire. That sustained fire can be for different reasons, either to stop an opponent that is attacking you or because you want to prepare the ground for an attack by your own ground forces. That is what I'm referring to in this statement. What I saw and witnessed in early June 1992 in Sarajevo was that the Bosnian Serb army was absolutely capable of directing very sustained and accurate fire on one particular target. On that occasion, it was the Marsal Tito barracks. That was sustained fire across two days and they hit that target again and again once they had found their range, which was also shown in -- in the story shown to the Court yesterday. That is what I'm referring to in the story in this -- in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have the same sort of interviews about the use of artillery weapons with Serb artillery men and commanders?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In October and November 1991, I spent a considerable amount of time with the forces of the Yugoslav Army around Vukovar, including quite a lot of time with artillery officers, and we filmed them actually firing those weapons and that -- as I recall, that was very much what they said as well, that they were giving sustained fire on certain parts of Vukovar because their own troops were engaged on the ground in Vukovar. They were there in conjunction with what those forces were doing on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember any names of any officer who explained to you how his unit operates?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Lukic. I met an awful lot of military officers in the former Yugoslavia. To remember all the names, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. What about the terrain in the US where you received the explanations? Was it anything like the terrain in Sarajevo? I don't think so ...

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't giving an explanation of the terrain in the United States. This was in Saudi Arabia where I met these American units. The terrain is different. The terrain is different in practically every war zone that I have been in. But the basis, as it was explained to me and as I have seen it used in various war zones of why you have artillery, that is basically the same. It can be much more complicated, of course, in mountainous terrain to observe directly the fire as it lands and therefore to make the corrections. But the basis is -- is, as far as I am aware, the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that the Serb artillery targeted various points in the city. You said that it was not the confrontation of front lines that were targeted. You say it was behind the lines. Is it true that artillery weapons are not kept on front lines, they are kept behind the lines, and that one cannot find a tank on the forward lines or a 120-millimetre mortar on the front line? They are to be found behind the lines; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Artillery weapons, would, indeed, usually be kept further from the front line. Tanks, however, I have absolutely seen close to the front lines, very, very close; usually behind some kind of a building but very, very close. And 120-millimetre mortars or smaller mortars can absolutely also be found on the front lines. It depends on the war zone, but I have seen them. Artillery, I would agree with you, is usually further back.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You spoke to us and showed us film 65 ter 22460E about the Unis towers. We don't have time to show them again. But you remember what I'm talking about; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You described it as the symbol of modern Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, those towers were described as a failed investment. But I want to ask you: Is it true that they were not inhabited. Nobody was living there, and there was no offices inside. Nobody either worked or lived there. They just stood there uncompleted, empty.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of people living in the Unis towers. I did, as I also testified to the Court yesterday, enter the Unis towers before they were hit and burnt, but I didn't -- I'm not aware whether all the offices were used or were not used. I am not aware whether it was or was not a failed investment. The Unis towers seemed to me a symbol of a new building and of a new time in Sarajevo, and that's why I came up with the phrase they were the symbol of modern Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, when you did enter the towers, did you notice that they were occupied by any businesses, offices, or something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By that stage, Your Honour, the war had already gone on for a while, and businesses had closed down, and, therefore, we didn't go into offices to check whether people were working there or not. Apart from that, their position, it was very exposed, as you could see in the film yesterday, and, therefore, anyone who did have a business in there would, I would imagine, have moved it by the stage when I was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At page 47, line 1, you say: "I did, as I also testified to the Court yesterday, enter the Unis towers before they were hit and burnt." And I ask you the question again: When you did enter them before they were hit and burnt, did you notice that any business was taking place in there or did you find any offices that simply -- I understand that you say people didn't live there but I want to know whether was this building occupied for business purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't actually see that, as I recall. We did meet certain people there when we arrived at the building and they took us upstairs, but whether there were any businesses still working there, I'm not aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. van Lynden.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, you said you entered one, if I remember well. Did you notice that in one of those towers the headquarters of the Territorial Defence was housed, of the Muslim forces? That it was the only group of people staying in these buildings?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that period, the headquarters of the Territorial Defence forces, as they were, indeed, still called, I'm aware of at a different location in Sarajevo, and we actually were taken to that location. The people that I encountered when we went to the Unis towers included at least two women who I don't think were members of the Territorial Defence forces. We didn't meet members of the Territorial Defence forces when I went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why do you think that women could not be members of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not dressed in military uniforms. They did not carry any kind of weaponry, nor did they tell us that they were members of the Territorial Defence forces. So I concluded that they were not. I am not saying that women cannot be in the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just to inform you, we received an answer from the ITSS and they confirmed that all our documents have been released. They say they are in e-court. The ITSS can see them, and they have no idea why we don't have them here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for the response. Are we able to see them now on e-court, as and when you are ready to go back to those exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
